aqa.3.13.2.1: Difference between analogue and digital signals

cards.q: Name the three terminals of a MOSFET, and say which one controls it.
cards.a: Drain, source and gate. The voltage between the gate and the source, VGS\displaystyle V_{GS}VGS​, controls the current between the drain and the source.

cards.q: For an N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, what is the threshold voltage Vth\displaystyle V_{th}Vth​?
cards.a: The smallest gate–source voltage at which the MOSFET starts to conduct between drain and source. Below it, the MOSFET is off.

cards.q: For a MOSFET, what are VDS\displaystyle V_{DS}VDS​, VGS\displaystyle V_{GS}VGS​ and IDSS\displaystyle I_{DSS}IDSS​?
cards.a: VDS\displaystyle V_{DS}VDS​: the voltage between drain and source. VGS\displaystyle V_{GS}VGS​: the voltage between gate and source. IDSS\displaystyle I_{DSS}IDSS​: the drain current when VGS\displaystyle V_{GS}VGS​ is zero, which for an enhancement-mode MOSFET is a very small leakage current.

cards.q: Why is a MOSFET useful as a switch driven by a logic circuit or a sensor?
cards.a: Its gate has a very high input resistance, so it draws almost no current from whatever drives it. A small gate voltage above the threshold can switch a large current through a load such as a motor or lamp.
cards.why: The gate is insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer.

cards.q: Describe the characteristic curve of a zener diode in reverse bias.
cards.a: Almost no current flows until the zener breakdown voltage is reached. The current then rises very steeply while the voltage across the diode stays almost constant.
cards.why: A minimum operating current is needed to keep it on the steep part of the curve.

cards.q: How is a zener diode connected to give a constant voltage?
cards.a: In reverse bias (cathode to the positive side), in series with a resistor across the supply. The output is taken across the diode and equals its breakdown voltage; the resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage and limits the current.
cards.why: It can also provide a fixed reference voltage, for example for a comparator.

cards.q: A 5.0 V zener diode is in series with a 350 Ω\displaystyle 350\ \Omega350 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply. Calculate the current in the resistor.
cards.a: 0.020 A (20 mA)
steps: Voltage across the resistor: 12−5.0=7.0 V\displaystyle 12 - 5.0 = 7.0\ \text{V}12−5.0=7.0 V.
I=VR=7.0350\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{7.0}{350}I=RV​=3507.0​
I=0.020 A\displaystyle I = 0.020\ \text{A}I=0.020 A

cards.q: How is a photodiode used in photo-conductive mode?
cards.a: It is reverse biased. In the dark only a tiny current flows; light falling on it releases charge carriers, giving a reverse current that is proportional to the light intensity.
cards.why: It responds very quickly, which suits it to detecting pulses in optical fibre systems.

cards.q: What does the spectral response curve of a photodiode show?
cards.a: How its sensitivity varies with the wavelength of the light. It peaks at one wavelength and falls away on either side, so a photodiode must be matched to the light source it is to detect.

cards.q: How is a photodiode used with a scintillator to detect atomic particles?
cards.a: A particle hitting the scintillator makes it give out a flash of light. The photodiode turns each flash into a pulse of current, which can be counted.

cards.q: What does a Hall effect sensor detect, and give two uses.
cards.a: Magnetic fields: its output voltage depends on the magnetic flux density through it. Uses: monitoring attitude (orientation relative to the Earth's field), and in a tachometer, counting the pulses as a magnet on a rotating shaft passes it.

cards.q: What is the difference between an analogue signal and a digital signal?
cards.a: An analogue signal can take any value in a continuous range. A digital signal has only two voltage levels, representing 1 and 0.

cards.q: What are a bit and a byte?
cards.a: A bit is a single binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte is a group of 8 bits.

cards.q: Describe how an analogue signal is converted into digital data.
cards.a: The signal's voltage is sampled at regular intervals. Each sample is quantised: rounded to the nearest of a fixed set of levels. The number of that level is sent as a binary code.
cards.why: Sending these codes as a stream of pulses is pulse code modulation.

cards.q: How do the sampling rate and the number of bits per sample affect the quality of a digitised signal?
cards.a: A higher sampling rate captures faster changes, so higher frequencies are reproduced. More bits per sample give more quantisation levels, so each sample is closer to the true voltage.
cards.why: The sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal.

cards.q: How many quantisation levels does an 8-bit sample allow?
cards.a: 256
steps: Number of levels =2n\displaystyle = 2^{n}=2n, where n\displaystyle nn is the number of bits.
28=256\displaystyle 2^{8} = 25628=256

cards.q: An audio signal is sampled at 40 kHz with 16 bits per sample. Calculate the bit rate.
cards.a: 6.4×105 bits per second\displaystyle 6.4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{bits per second}6.4×105 bits per second
steps: Bit rate = sampling rate × bits per sample.
=40×103×16\displaystyle = 40 \times 10^{3} \times 16=40×103×16
=6.4×105 bit s−1\displaystyle = 6.4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{bit s}^{-1}=6.4×105 bit s−1

cards.q: Explain why a digital signal can be recovered from noise but an analogue signal cannot.
cards.a: A digital signal has only two levels, so it can be regenerated.
marks: Noise adds unwanted random variations to any signal.
A digital signal only has to be recognised as high or low, so a noisy pulse can be regenerated as a clean one.
In an analogue signal the noise cannot be told apart from the signal, so amplifying the signal amplifies the noise too.

cards.q: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of transmitting a signal in digital form.
cards.a: Advantages: noise can be removed by regenerating the pulses, and the data can be processed, stored, compressed and checked for errors by computer. Disadvantage: some information is lost in sampling and quantising, and a digital signal needs a greater bandwidth.

cards.q: Write the equation for the resonant frequency of a parallel LC circuit.
cards.a: f0=12πLC\displaystyle f_{0} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}f0​=2πLC​1​

cards.q: In the analogy between an LC circuit and a mass–spring system, what do the inductance and the capacitance correspond to?
cards.a: Inductance corresponds to the mass; capacitance corresponds to the spring.
cards.why: Energy swaps between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field, as it does between the spring's elastic energy and the mass's kinetic energy.

cards.q: Define the Q factor of an LC filter, and say what the bandwidth fB\displaystyle f_{B}fB​ is.
cards.a: Q=f0fB\displaystyle Q = \frac{f_{0}}{f_{B}}Q=fB​f0​​. The bandwidth fB\displaystyle f_{B}fB​ is the range of frequencies between the two points on the energy response curve where the energy is 50% of its peak value.
cards.why: A high Q means a sharp, narrow peak: a more selective filter.

cards.q: An LC filter has a resonant frequency of 5.0 kHz and a bandwidth of 250 Hz. Calculate its Q factor.
cards.a: 20
steps: Q=f0fB=5000250\displaystyle Q = \frac{f_{0}}{f_{B}} = \frac{5000}{250}Q=fB​f0​​=2505000​
Q=20\displaystyle Q = 20Q=20

cards.q: State two characteristics of an ideal operational amplifier.
cards.a: Infinite open-loop gain, and infinite input resistance, so no current flows into either input.

cards.q: Write the open-loop transfer function of a real operational amplifier.
cards.a: Vout=AOL(V+−V−)\displaystyle V_{out} = A_{OL}(V_{+} - V_{-})Vout​=AOL​(V+​−V−​), where AOL\displaystyle A_{OL}AOL​ is the open-loop gain, V+\displaystyle V_{+}V+​ the voltage at the non-inverting input and V−\displaystyle V_{-}V−​ the voltage at the inverting input.
cards.why: The output can never go beyond the supply voltages: it saturates.

cards.q: How does an operational amplifier behave when it is used as a comparator?
cards.a: It compares its two input voltages. Because the open-loop gain is so large, the output saturates: close to the positive supply voltage if V+\displaystyle V_{+}V+​ is greater than V−\displaystyle V_{-}V−​, and close to the negative supply voltage if V+\displaystyle V_{+}V+​ is less than V−\displaystyle V_{-}V−​.

cards.q: Write the gain of an inverting amplifier.
cards.a: VoutVin=−RfRin\displaystyle \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = -\frac{R_{f}}{R_{in}}Vin​Vout​​=−Rin​Rf​​
cards.why: The minus sign means the output is inverted.

cards.q: What is meant by a virtual earth in an inverting amplifier?
cards.a: The inverting input stays at almost 0 V, although it is not connected to earth. The non-inverting input is at 0 V, and with a huge open-loop gain the two inputs must be at practically the same voltage for the output not to saturate.

cards.q: Derive the gain of an inverting amplifier using virtual-earth analysis.
cards.a: VoutVin=−RfRin\displaystyle \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = -\frac{R_{f}}{R_{in}}Vin​Vout​​=−Rin​Rf​​
steps: The inverting input is a virtual earth, at 0 V. So the current in the input resistor is I=VinRin\displaystyle I = \frac{V_{in}}{R_{in}}I=Rin​Vin​​.
The input resistance is infinite, so no current enters the amplifier: the same current flows through Rf\displaystyle R_{f}Rf​.
The voltage across Rf\displaystyle R_{f}Rf​ is 0−Vout\displaystyle 0 - V_{out}0−Vout​, so I=−VoutRf\displaystyle I = \frac{-V_{out}}{R_{f}}I=Rf​−Vout​​.

Equating: VinRin=−VoutRf\displaystyle \frac{V_{in}}{R_{in}} = \frac{-V_{out}}{R_{f}}Rin​Vin​​=Rf​−Vout​​, so VoutVin=−RfRin\displaystyle \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = -\frac{R_{f}}{R_{in}}Vin​Vout​​=−Rin​Rf​​.

Vout=−2.0 V\displaystyle V_{out} = -2.0\ \text{V}Vout​=−2.0 V

cards.a: VoutVin=1+RfR1\displaystyle \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = 1 + \frac{R_{f}}{R_{1}}Vin​Vout​​=1+R1​Rf​​
cards.why: The gain is positive and never less than 1.

cards.q: State the relationship between the gain and the bandwidth of a real operational amplifier.
cards.a: gain × bandwidth = constant for a given device. Increasing the gain reduces the range of frequencies it can amplify.
cards.why: Its frequency response curve is flat up to the bandwidth, then the gain falls.

cards.q: An operational amplifier has a gain–bandwidth product of 1.0×106 Hz\displaystyle 1.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{Hz}1.0×106 Hz. Calculate its bandwidth when it is used with a gain of 50.
cards.a: 2.0×104 Hz\displaystyle 2.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{Hz}2.0×104 Hz
steps: bandwidth=gain–bandwidth productgain=1.0×10650\displaystyle \text{bandwidth} = \frac{\text{gain–bandwidth product}}{\text{gain}} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{6}}{50}bandwidth=gaingain–bandwidth product​=501.0×106​
=2.0×104 Hz\displaystyle = 2.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{Hz}=2.0×104 Hz

cards.q: Give three ways in which a real operational amplifier falls short of an ideal one.
cards.a: Its open-loop gain is large but not infinite, and falls at high frequencies. Its input resistance is not infinite, so a tiny current flows into the inputs. Its output cannot exceed the supply voltages.

cards.q: Write the Boolean expressions for NOT A, A AND B, and A OR B.
cards.a: NOT A: A‾\displaystyle \overline{A}A. A AND B: A⋅B\displaystyle A \cdot BA⋅B. A OR B: A+B\displaystyle A + BA+B.

cards.q: State when the output is 1 for a two-input AND gate, OR gate, NAND gate and NOR gate.
cards.a: AND: only when both inputs are 1. OR: when at least one input is 1. NAND: unless both inputs are 1. NOR: only when both inputs are 0.

cards.q: When is the output of a two-input EOR (exclusive OR) gate 1?
cards.a: When the two inputs are different: one is 1 and the other is 0.

cards.q: A logic circuit has output Q=A‾⋅B\displaystyle Q = \overline{A} \cdot BQ=A⋅B. For which inputs is Q\displaystyle QQ equal to 1?
cards.a: Only when A = 0 and B = 1.
cards.why: The circuit is a NOT gate on input A, feeding an AND gate with B.

cards.q: What are the clock, reset and up/down inputs of a counter for?
cards.a: Clock: the count changes by one on each clock pulse. Reset: returns the count to zero. Up/down: sets whether the count goes up or down.

cards.q: How do a binary counter and a BCD counter differ?
cards.a: A 4-bit binary counter counts from 0000 to 1111 (0 to 15) and then starts again. A BCD counter counts from 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9) and then resets to zero, so each counter stores one decimal digit.

cards.q: Describe the output sequence of a 4-bit Johnson counter.
cards.a: On each clock pulse the bits shift along one place, and the inverse of the last bit is fed back to the first. The outputs fill with 1s and then with 0s: 0000, 1000, 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, 0001, then repeat. That is 8 states, with only one bit changing at a time.

cards.q: How can a binary counter be made into a modulo-6 counter?
cards.a: Logic gates detect when the outputs reach 6 (binary 110) and drive the reset pin. Here an AND gate on the two outputs that are 1 does it. The count then runs 0 to 5 and resets: six states.

cards.q: What is an astable, and what is it used for?
cards.a: A circuit with no stable state: its output switches continually between high and low. It is an oscillator, used to provide clock pulses.
cards.why: Its frequency is set by an external resistor–capacitor network.

cards.q: Define the duty cycle and the mark-to-space ratio of a pulse train.
cards.a: Duty cycle: the time the output is high as a percentage of the period. Mark-to-space ratio: the time high (mark) divided by the time low (space).

cards.q: The output of an astable is high for 3.0 ms and low for 1.0 ms in each cycle. Calculate its frequency.
cards.a: 250 Hz
cards.why: Its duty cycle is 75% and its mark-to-space ratio is 3.
steps: Period: 3.0+1.0=4.0 ms\displaystyle 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0\ \text{ms}3.0+1.0=4.0 ms.
f=1T=14.0×10−3\displaystyle f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}f=T1​=4.0×10−31​
f=250 Hz\displaystyle f = 250\ \text{Hz}f=250 Hz

cards.q: List the stages of a real-time communication system, in order.
cards.a: Input transducer → modulator → amplifier → transmitter → transmission path → receiver → amplifier → demodulator → output transducer.
cards.why: The input transducer turns the information into an electrical signal; the modulator puts it onto a carrier.

cards.q: Give two advantages of optic fibre over metal wire for transmitting data.
cards.a: A much higher data transmission rate, because light has a far higher frequency and so offers more bandwidth. It is more secure and free of electrical interference; signals also weaken less, so fewer repeaters are needed.

cards.q: How do ground waves and sky waves travel beyond the horizon?
cards.a: Ground waves (long wavelengths) diffract around the curve of the Earth's surface. Sky waves are refracted and reflected by the ionosphere back down to the ground.

cards.q: Why does a communications satellite use different frequencies for its up-link and down-link?
cards.a: So that its receiver is not de-sensed: the strong signal it transmits would otherwise swamp the very weak signal it is receiving.
cards.why: Satellite links use microwave frequencies, of the order of gigahertz, which pass through the ionosphere.

cards.q: What is time-division multiplexing?
cards.a: Sending several signals along one channel by giving each a short time slot in turn. The receiver, kept in step with the transmitter, separates the slots back into the original signals.

cards.q: What is the difference between amplitude modulation and frequency modulation?
cards.a: In AM, the amplitude of the carrier wave is varied by the information signal and its frequency stays constant. In FM, the frequency of the carrier is varied and its amplitude stays constant.

cards.q: On a graph of voltage against time for an AM signal, how do you find the carrier frequency and the information frequency?
cards.a: The carrier frequency comes from the period of the rapid oscillations. The information frequency comes from the period of the slowly varying outline (envelope) of the peaks.

cards.q: An AM signal carries information with a maximum frequency of 4.5 kHz. Calculate the bandwidth needed.
cards.a: 9.0 kHz
steps: For AM: bandwidth=2fM\displaystyle \text{bandwidth} = 2f_{M}bandwidth=2fM​
=2×4.5=9.0 kHz\displaystyle = 2 \times 4.5 = 9.0\ \text{kHz}=2×4.5=9.0 kHz

cards.q: An FM signal has a frequency deviation of 75 kHz and a maximum information frequency of 15 kHz. Calculate the bandwidth needed.
cards.a: 180 kHz
cards.why: FM needs far more bandwidth than AM, but is much less affected by noise.
steps: For FM: bandwidth=2(Δf+fM)\displaystyle \text{bandwidth} = 2(\Delta f + f_{M})bandwidth=2(Δf+fM​)
=2×(75+15)\displaystyle = 2 \times (75 + 15)=2×(75+15)
=180 kHz\displaystyle = 180\ \text{kHz}=180 kHz
